articles.title: Watching Wednesday's solar eclipse? The glasses you need to protect your eyes
articles.excerpt: Rochdale is preparing for Wednesday's major partial solar eclipse - but ordinary sunglasses are not safe. Here's what to look for in eclipse glasses and how to watch safely.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale is preparing for one of the most spectacular astronomical events visible from Britain in years, with a major partial solar eclipse due to darken the skies on Wednesday 12 August.

But anyone planning to look up needs to get one thing sorted before Wednesday evening: ordinary sunglasses are not safe for watching a solar eclipse.

Specialist solar-eclipse glasses are designed to reduce the Sun's radiation to a level suitable for direct viewing. The important marking to look for is ISO 12312-2, the international safety standard covering filters used for direct observation of the Sun.

The Royal Observatory Greenwich advises eclipse watchers to use purpose-made solar viewing protection. Eclipse glasses should be inspected before use and should not be used if the filter is scratched, torn, punctured or otherwise damaged.

WHAT SHOULD YOU BUY?

Rochdale Daily has found Astral Solar Eclipse Paper Glasses from Absolute Eclipse, designed specifically for direct solar viewing. The retailer states that the glasses comply with EN ISO 12312-2:2015 and use specialist solar-filter material.

Single pairs are advertised at approximately £4.30 based on the retailer's euro price and current exchange rates, although the exact sterling amount charged may vary with the exchange rate and payment provider. Multipacks are also available for families and groups.

Rochdale Daily may receive a commission if readers purchase through the link above. This does not increase the price paid by the customer.

WHY AREN'T SUNGLASSES ENOUGH?

Even extremely dark conventional sunglasses are designed for everyday daylight, not staring directly at the Sun. During an eclipse, the reduction in visible daylight can also create a false sense that looking towards the Sun has become safer. It has not.

Looking directly at the Sun without appropriate protection can damage the retina at the back of the eye. Crucially, retinal injury may occur without immediate pain, meaning somebody may not realise damage has occurred while they are watching.

Purpose-made eclipse glasses meeting the appropriate solar-viewing standard or an indirect viewing method such as a pinhole projector should therefore be used.

CHECK YOUR GLASSES BEFORE PUTTING THEM ON

Before Wednesday's eclipse, check the solar-filter material carefully. If you find scratches, holes, tears, punctures or other damage, do not use that pair.

Put your eclipse glasses on before looking towards the Sun and turn away from the Sun before removing them. Children should be supervised to make sure the glasses remain correctly positioned while they are looking upwards.

There is another important distinction: eclipse glasses are intended for unaided viewing with your eyes. They should not be used to look through binoculars, telescopes or camera lenses. Optical equipment concentrates sunlight and requires correctly fitted specialist solar filters designed for that equipment.

WHAT IF YOU CAN'T GET GLASSES IN TIME?

You can still experience the eclipse without looking directly at the Sun. A simple pinhole projector allows sunlight to pass through a small opening and project an image of the partially eclipsed Sun onto another surface.

Whatever method you choose, do not improvise with ordinary sunglasses, tinted glass or homemade eye filters.

WHEN CAN ROCHDALE SEE IT?

The eclipse takes place on Wednesday 12 August, beginning in the early evening and reaching maximum coverage shortly after 7pm in the Greater Manchester area. Around nine-tenths of the Sun is expected to be obscured at maximum, weather permitting.

It should create an extraordinary sight across Rochdale - but the most important preparation is making sure everyone watching has suitable eye protection before looking towards the Sun.

articles.title: Rochdale Science Initiative Launches Summer Holiday Programme
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale Science Initiative's Summer Holiday Activities and Food programme is now underway, providing educational activities for local children during the summer break.
articles.content_html:
A programme called the Summer Holiday Activities and Food (HAF) has been launched by the Rochdale Science Initiative C.I.C. The initiative is funded by the Department for Education and aims to provide educational activities and meals for children during the summer holidays.

The programme is currently in its second day and is designed to engage children in various science-related activities. It seeks to combine learning with fun, ensuring that children have a productive summer break.

Dhruv Goel, a representative of the Rochdale Science Initiative, highlighted the importance of such programmes in supporting children's education and well-being during the holidays. The initiative aims to reach as many local children as possible.

The HAF programme is expected to run throughout the summer, offering a range of activities that promote learning and healthy eating. Parents are encouraged to register their children to take part in the activities.

articles.title: Developer Appeals Refusal of Student Housing Scheme in Middleton
articles.excerpt: A developer has appealed a council decision to refuse plans for student accommodation at a former nursing home in Middleton, following significant local opposition.
articles.content_html:
A developer has appealed a council decision to refuse plans for converting an old nursing home in Middleton into student accommodation. The planning committee at Rochdale town hall rejected the proposal for the former Briarmede Care Home in June, citing concerns over the impact on the character of the area and a lack of need for additional student housing.

Al-Sadiq Academy aimed to create 11 en-suite bedrooms and two studio flats at the Rochdale Road site. Following the refusal, the academy has requested the Planning Inspectorate to review the decision. The developer argued that the proposed common area would be suitable for students, featuring a dining hall, games room, study areas, kitchens, computer rooms, changing facilities, and a library.

The proposal faced significant opposition, with around 400 objectors claiming it was a 'backdoor' attempt to establish a mosque and wedding venue, a claim that Al-Sadiq Academy has denied. Members of the planning committee expressed similar concerns, with Coun Tom Besford stating that many residents did not believe the site would ultimately serve as student accommodation.

The planning committee ultimately decided to refuse the application, stating that the change of use from a nursing home to student accommodation would adversely affect the character of the area and that there was insufficient evidence to support the need for such housing. The Planning Inspectorate will now review the council's decision, and their ruling will be final.

articles.title: Is ketamine becoming a problem in Rochdale? Health leaders warn of a growing concern
articles.excerpt: Health professionals are warning of the growing harms associated with ketamine as national use rises. But what does the picture look like in Rochdale, and why are experts becoming increasingly concerned?
articles.content_html:
Ketamine was once regarded primarily as a nightclub drug, but health professionals, police and addiction specialists say its use has changed dramatically over the past decade. Increasingly, the drug is being used by younger people in a wider range of settings, prompting growing concern about its impact on physical and mental health.

While there is no publicly available evidence to suggest Rochdale has a ketamine problem significantly worse than other parts of Greater Manchester, local authorities recognise substance misuse as an important public health issue and have included drug-related harm as a key priority in the borough's long-term prevention strategy. Rochdale's Preventing Drug and Alcohol Harm Strategy highlights the need to reduce drug-related harm through prevention, early intervention, treatment and recovery services.

Ketamine is a Class B controlled drug in the UK. Originally developed as a medical anaesthetic, it produces feelings of detachment and hallucinations when used recreationally. In recent years, it has become increasingly popular because it is often cheaper than cocaine and MDMA, while users mistakenly believe it to be a 'safer' drug.

National evidence suggests that perception is dangerously wrong. The Home Office's latest wastewater analysis estimates ketamine consumption has increased substantially in England in recent years, making it one of the country's most commonly consumed illegal drugs after cocaine.

Doctors are particularly concerned about the long-term physical effects. Repeated ketamine use can cause irreversible damage to the bladder and urinary tract, a condition sometimes referred to as 'ketamine bladder' or ketamine-induced cystitis. Heavy users may experience severe pain, frequent urination, bleeding and, in the most serious cases, permanent bladder damage requiring reconstructive surgery. Medical specialists have reported a significant increase in young patients requiring treatment for these complications.

Mental health professionals also warn that regular ketamine use can lead to dependency, memory problems, anxiety, depression and episodes of psychosis in some individuals. Because the drug affects perception and coordination, users are also at increased risk of accidents, injuries and dangerous behaviour while intoxicated.

Locally, Rochdale Borough Council's Joint Strategic Needs Assessment identifies substance misuse among young adults as an ongoing public health challenge. Hospital admission rates linked to substance misuse among young people remain broadly similar to the national average, while the council notes that vulnerable groups are at greater risk of developing drug-related problems.

Although official figures are not routinely broken down by individual drug at borough level, professionals working in addiction services across Greater Manchester say ketamine now features far more frequently than it did a decade ago. Nationally, the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs concluded earlier this year that misuse is increasing and recommended strengthening education, prevention and treatment services while keeping ketamine as a Class B drug.

Parents are encouraged to be aware of the warning signs. These can include sudden mood changes, poor concentration, unexplained urinary problems, nosebleeds caused by snorting powder, secrecy around friendships, declining school or college attendance and unexplained financial difficulties. None of these signs alone necessarily indicate drug use, but experts advise early conversations and support where concerns exist.

Support is available for anyone struggling with drug use. Rochdale residents can access confidential help through local drug and alcohol treatment services without fear of judgement. Health professionals stress that seeking support early greatly improves the chances of recovery and helps prevent long-term physical damage.

The message from health leaders is clear. While ketamine may still carry an image as a recreational party drug, the evidence increasingly shows it can have devastating consequences for both physical and mental health. Prevention, education and early intervention remain the most effective ways of protecting young people across Rochdale borough from the lasting harm associated with its misuse.

articles.title: GCSE results day 2026: What Rochdale parents need to know – and why one set of grades doesn't define a future
articles.excerpt: From college offers to apprenticeships and changing employer expectations, here's everything Rochdale parents need to know before GCSE results day.
articles.content_html:
Thousands of teenagers across Rochdale borough will soon collect one of the most important envelopes of their young lives as GCSE results day approaches.

For many families, results day brings a mixture of excitement, nerves and uncertainty. Parents naturally want the best for their children, but education experts say GCSEs are increasingly becoming just one of several routes into higher education, apprenticeships and long-term careers rather than the single deciding factor they were once perceived to be.

This year's GCSE results will be released on Thursday 20 August, with schools across Rochdale opening to allow students to collect their grades and speak with teachers about their next steps. Students will receive provisional results before certificates are issued later in the year.

For many teenagers, the next destination has already been decided through conditional offers from sixth forms and colleges. Most colleges will honour offers provided students meet the required grades, while admissions teams are usually available on results day to discuss alternatives if results are different from those expected.

Compared with a decade ago, today's post-16 education landscape is far more flexible. Alongside traditional A Levels, students can now choose from T Levels, vocational qualifications, apprenticeships and technical training, giving young people far more options depending on their interests and career ambitions. Greater Manchester has also continued expanding the Greater Manchester Baccalaureate (MBacc), designed to place technical education on an equal footing with academic study while creating clearer pathways into local industries.

Parents often ask whether GCSEs still matter.

The answer is yes—but perhaps not in the way they once did.

GCSEs remain important because they open doors. Most sixth forms, colleges, universities and apprenticeship providers require passes in English Language and Mathematics, while many A Level courses ask for a minimum grade in the subject students wish to study. Employers also continue to value GCSEs as evidence of literacy, numeracy and commitment, particularly when recruiting school leavers with little previous work experience. Ofqual has described GCSEs as a 'passport to opportunity', providing access to further education, apprenticeships and employment.

However, the employment market has changed dramatically. Increasingly, recruiters say experience, practical skills, communication, teamwork and attitude become far more important than GCSE grades as careers progress.

Recruitment specialists consistently report that while GCSEs may be used as an initial screening tool for younger applicants, employers recruiting experienced candidates are far more interested in work history, achievements, technical skills and professional qualifications. In sectors such as construction, logistics, digital technology, engineering, health and social care, apprenticeships have become an increasingly respected route into well-paid careers.

That does not mean students should dismiss their exams. Strong GCSE results can provide greater choice and flexibility, particularly for competitive sixth forms, universities and professional careers such as medicine, dentistry and law. But equally, disappointing grades do not prevent someone building a successful future.

Parents are also encouraged to remember that results day is only one moment in a much longer journey. Colleges regularly help students who narrowly miss entry requirements by suggesting alternative courses, foundation programmes or vocational pathways that still lead towards the same career goals.

For students who do not achieve the grade 4 pass in English or Mathematics, the law requires them to continue studying those subjects alongside most post-16 courses until they achieve the qualification or turn 18. While this can initially feel disappointing, many students successfully improve their grades during college.

Perhaps the biggest change in recent years has been the growing recognition that success comes in many different forms. University is no longer viewed as the only prestigious route after school. Degree apprenticeships, higher apprenticeships and technical qualifications now offer opportunities to earn a salary while gaining nationally recognised qualifications, often avoiding the student debt associated with traditional university study.

For parents, experts recommend focusing on support rather than pressure. Results day can be emotional regardless of the outcome. Celebrating achievements, discussing options calmly and remembering that there are always alternative pathways can help young people make confident decisions about their future.

Whether a student achieves straight grade 9s or faces unexpected disappointment, GCSE results represent the beginning of the next chapter rather than the end of the story. Across Rochdale borough this summer, thousands of young people will take their next step towards sixth form, college, apprenticeships, employment or technical training—and for many, the opportunities available today are broader than ever before.

articles.title: Norden's hidden gem: Manchester fine dining right here in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Forget the drive into Manchester. Stocco in Norden is proving that one of Greater Manchester's finest dining experiences can be found right here in Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
When people think of fine dining, they often picture Manchester city centre, Spinningfields or the Northern Quarter. But tucked away in the village of Norden is a restaurant quietly proving that you don't have to travel into the city for an exceptional dining experience.

Stocco, on Edenfield Road, has rapidly established itself as one of Rochdale's standout restaurants, combining contemporary Italian cuisine with stylish surroundings and attentive service that would not look out of place in one of Manchester's best-known dining districts.

Occupying the former Mezbaan site, the restaurant has transformed the building into a modern Italian-inspired venue featuring elegant interiors, a spacious cocktail bar, outdoor terrace seating and room for more than 100 diners. Free parking is available nearby, making it an attractive alternative to the expense and inconvenience of travelling into Manchester for a special meal.

The menu blends traditional Italian cooking with modern British influences, offering everything from freshly prepared pasta and seafood dishes to premium steaks, artisan antipasti and seasonal chef's specials. Ingredients are sourced from local suppliers wherever possible, while speciality products are imported directly from Italy to retain authentic flavours.

Whether you're looking for a relaxed lunch, an evening celebration, cocktails with friends or a romantic meal, Stocco offers a level of quality and atmosphere that many diners would normally expect to find much closer to Manchester city centre.

Its arrival has also helped strengthen Norden's growing reputation as one of Rochdale borough's premier destinations for independent food and drink. Over recent years, the village has developed a thriving hospitality scene, attracting visitors from across Greater Manchester, Rossendale and Lancashire who are increasingly discovering what local residents have known for years.

Since opening, Stocco has built a loyal following, with many customers praising both the quality of the food and the welcoming service. The restaurant has become a popular choice for birthdays, anniversaries, family gatherings and business lunches, while its stylish décor and contemporary feel have made it equally appealing for casual dining.

Perhaps one of Stocco's biggest advantages is convenience. Instead of battling Manchester traffic, paying city-centre parking charges or relying on trains and trams, diners can enjoy a high-end restaurant experience just minutes from Rochdale town centre.

For residents of Rochdale, Bury, Rossendale and the surrounding areas, it is another reminder that outstanding dining experiences don't always require a trip into the city. Sometimes, one of the region's best-kept culinary secrets is much closer to home.

So, the next time you're considering booking a table in Manchester, it might be worth looking north instead. Tucked away in the heart of Norden is a restaurant that delivers city-quality dining with village charm—making it one of Rochdale's true hidden gems.
